title: Ash-Sharh: with hardship, ease
hook: with hardship comes ease, said twice (94:5–6)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ash-Sharh, the opened chest and the lifted burden. Your line was the burden lifts.

Some sentences get written on hospital whiteboards, taped above desks during exam season, texted at three in the morning to a friend whose marriage just ended. One short Qur'anic line turns up in places like these: in Arabic calligraphy on living-room walls, on phone lock screens, on the last page of a student's notebook. It's said twice in a row, and the way it's worded is more hopeful than a quick reading suggests.
screen: `ON WHITEBOARDS, DESKS, LOCK SCREENS.` → `SAID TWICE IN A ROW.` → `MORE HOPEFUL THAN IT SOUNDS.`

segments.voice: After the opened chest, the lifted burden and the raised name, the surah says, in Pickthall's translation: But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease. Notice the first small word: ma'a, with. Not after hardship. With it. The ease isn't only waiting at the end of the hard thing; it's already inside it, traveling alongside. Even a hard stretch often has something that holds a person up: a friend who shows up, a night of good sleep, a moment of laughter at the hospital. Now the grammar, which classical commentators dwelt on. In Arabic, hardship is al-'usr, with the word the: the hardship, the same one both times. But ease is yusr, without the: an ease, and then another ease. The same hardship, said twice, meets two different eases. A saying reported from early Muslims puts it this way: one hardship will never overcome two eases. Scholars discuss how firmly that saying traces back, but commentators still teach the reading of the grammar. Then the surah ends with what to do: when you're free of one task, keep working, and turn to your Lord with longing. Not sit and wait for ease. Keep going, toward Him. Tradition places this surah in the hard years in Mecca, when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had few followers and the pressure was heavy. It didn't promise that the hardship would vanish. It promised company for it.
screen: `MA'A — WITH, NOT AFTER.` · `THE HARDSHIP, AND AN EASE.` · `ONE HARDSHIP, TWO EASES.` · `WHEN FREE, KEEP WORKING, TOWARD HIM.` · then, large: `WITH HARDSHIP, EASE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hard thing you're in the middle of right now, and without trying to fix it, look for what's traveling alongside it: a person who's helped, something you've learned, a small good that came only because of this. Name one ease, then look again for a second.
Ash-Sharh. The opened chest, and the surah that says twice: with hardship comes ease. Today's word.
Your line: with hardship, ease. One hardship, and more than one ease. That's day one hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims often quote 94:5–6, inna ma'a al-'usri yusra, to comfort each other in illness, loss and hard times, and the verse is common in calligraphy in homes and on cards.

fork.setup: you've just finished a hard task, and ease has come. what does the end of the surah say to do?
options: keep working, and turn to your Lord with longing
fork.reveal: when you're free, keep striving, and turn to your Lord (94:7–8). the ease isn't a stopping point.

original.note: Arabic: an ease, indefinite; set against al-'usr, the hardship, in 94:5–6.

trapdoor: what you thought: after bad times come good times.
what it means: ease comes with hardship, alongside it, and the verse is repeated for emphasis.

what a scholar hears: definite al-'usr repeated is one hardship, indefinite yusr repeated is two eases; the saying 'one hardship won't overcome two eases' is attributed to Umar and Ibn Abbas, with chains scholars discuss.

notes: Please confirm the exact Pickthall wording of 94:5–6.

The 'two eases' saying: attributed to Umar, Ibn Abbas and in some reports the Prophet; chains are weak or mursal. The script says 'a saying reported from early Muslims' and that scholars discuss its chain.
94:7–8 paraphrased; readings differ (e.g. 'when you finish your prayer, stand in supplication').
